messages.subject: Re: Bayes Factor in mirt anova
messages.body_plain:
Dear Phil,

first of all: thank you very much for this great package!

Right now I'm trying to get my head around the output of the anova()-function when applied to two models with prior specification of the intercept. I'm confused about your statement above:

"The anova organizes the input objects such that the comparison is always nested based on the degrees of freedom. So it will always test whether the model with more df fits worse than the one with more. Hence, the bayes factor is always organized to test whether the less restrictive model is more likely than the less restrictive."

Does anova() test whether the model with fewer or with more df fits worse? And does the BF organized to test whether the less restrictive model is more likely or the more restrictive model?

Best
Marvin

>

It tests whether the model with fewer degrees of freedom fits worse than the less constrained model. Though an equivalent interpretation is whether the less constrained model fits 'unusually better' than the more constrained base model with fewer df.

Phil

messages.body_plain:

The direction of location parameter is GGUM is somewhat arbitary. I think that may be the reason why you see "perfect" negative correlation.

On Thursday, November 28, 2019 at 10:38:37 AM UTC-6, Kiff Cu wrote:
> Hi Dear Chalmers.
> I use ideal point model fordata with 15 six point Likert type items (the scale measures cognitive flexibility).
> The attached file contains the results. Everything was ok with the results except the correlation between GGUM model based estimates of ability and alternative dominance models (GRM and GPCM) is almost perfectly negative. I know that it is possible to reaching such kind of result because the probability of endoring an option is defined differently by dominance and ideal point models. But such kind of "perfect" contrast make me to be sceptic on whether or not I made something wrong.  Also, even everything is ok with this result, I couldn't figure out how to interpret this results. In the literature, there are some articles where theta estimates from different models are perfectly (positively) correlated.
> I really appreciate if you (or somebody who have experience on ideal point models) give some suggestions and directions for interpreting the results.
> Best regards.

messages.subject: Re: information curve for partial items
messages.body_plain:
Dear Phil,

Thanks for your previous reply to my question a long time ago, and I have been thinking about superimposing the information curve between two methods lately. My hypothesis is that items using method A will be better in assessing a construct at a higher level, and items using method B will be better in assessing a construct at a lower level. Items from both method A and method B will load on the same construct. Is there a way to superimposing the two information curves (from two methods) on the same figure, so that I can check if my hypothesis is valid or not? Currently, I only know how to request information curves from all items related to Method A or from all items related to Method B separately. Much appreciate your help!

Best regards,
Chester

messages.subject: GPCM with lacking linked/common items
messages.body_plain:
Dear Phil and the forum,

I am attempting to apply a GPCM model using the mirt package to a dataset with the following characteristics:

-          The dataset has 9 items in total, all of which measure Grade 2 maths skills

-          These 9 items are formed of 3 test sets, each of which contains one 6-level item and two dichotomous items

-          The (approx. 40,000) children contained in the dataset were all randomly assigned to 1 of the 3 test sets.

-          No child has answered all 9 items. Indeed, no child that has answered questions from one test set has also answered any questions from any other test set. (I therefore have no linked/common items between any of the test sets.)

Using the mirt function on this dataset (“IRTset”) runs fine and produces logical results, from the command:

expmodel <- mirt(data = IRTset, model = 1, itemtype = "gpcm")

I noticed that in a response to another question on working with tests where there are no common items, you said “if you can assume that the latent traits across groups are identical theoretically, then the items are technically already equated” (https://groups.google.com/forum/?nomobile=true#!searchin/mirt-package/linked$20items%7Csort:date/mirt-package/ib_tHG_LqlY/AmGu2vvoBgAJ). I am happy enough to assume that mathematics ability (my trait of interest) is identical between 'groups' due to the random assignment of test set 1, 2 or 3 to each child taking the test.

I would be hugely grateful if you could let me know:

-          If it is illogical for any reason to apply the mirt function in the manner described above, given the nature of my dataset

-          If there are any specific checks before/after applying the mirt function that I need to do, given the nature of my data, beyond the following basics: trace and test info plots; Yen’s Q3; summary(expmodel); and, coef(expmodel, IRTpars = T)

Thank you in advance for any help, and please let me know if it is useful for me to clarify anything above. Please also feel free to just refer me to some relevant literature that I have missed.

Joe

messages.subject: Re: A problem about non-compensatory model
messages.body_plain:
You probably want to use the expbeta distribution, not the beta one. This one is still a beta with the usual inputs, whoever the input value is transformed according to an inverse logit link, which is important because internally mirt reparameterizes the g terms into logits, and estimates those instead (it's much easier to work with when using quasi-Newton optimizers for parameters with bounded spaces). There's discussion of this parameterization on this forum, as well as in a few of my published articles (also often reference in the package documentation). HTH.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: information curve for partial items
messages.body_plain:
Sure, but you'd have to construct such plots manually since mirt doesn't do this out of the box. iteminfo() is likely what you want to inspect, though note that in general simply drawing the tracelines could be a little misleading if your sample size isn't sufficiently large due to the sampling variability of the curves. You might have to think of a way to generate sets of variability for the plot, such as via bootstrapping or parametric draws from the posterior distribution (mirt has functions to do both things) to include confidence intervals around the associated information functions. Something like what the following does:

library(mirt)
x <- mirt(Science, 1, SE=TRUE)
plot(x, type='info', MI=100)

HTH.

Phil

>

>

messages.body_plain:
Hi Phil,

I am fitting rsm, pcm, gpcm, and ggum models to a set of datasets, and received the warning that "item re-scored so that all values are within a distance of 1". Can you help how to go about avoiding this?

Thanks!

On Wednesday, February 7, 2018 at 1:27:55 PM UTC-5, Phil Chalmers wrote:

> The idea is that if the observed item's unique responses are of the form:
>
> c(1,2,4) == unique(item)
>
> where for some reason it's clear that the 3rd category was never endorsed, then mirt will change all instances of 4 to 3
>
> c(1,2,3) == unique(item)
>
> Hence, all the unique values are 1 unit appart. The reason is somewhat technical, but because IRT models assume categorical relationships the values of the coding scheme should be relevant, and this just helps the internal arguments determine the ordering and spacing of the categories. For most IRT models, such as the graded response, nominal, etc, this translation is irrelevant. For other models where the scoring scheme is meaningful (such as in a partial credit model) then the fixed scoring coefficients would need to be overwritten at the time of estimation. So, unless you are using itemtype = 'gpcm', then I wouldn't worry.

>
> Phil
>

> On Wed, Feb 7, 2018 at 12:29 PM, Ki Cole <ki....@okstate.edu> wrote:

> > I am doing a study of polytomous IRT, specifically studying situations with low response rates. I am trying to better understand the "Item re-scored so that all values are within a distance of 1."
> >
> > You respond, "If some responses are obviously missing then all higher scores are changed so that they are equally spaced."
> >
> > Can you provide more insight into this adjustment or where I am read about it further. I'm traced the mirt source code, but I'm not able to locate the technicalities of this change.
> >
> > Thank you.
> > Ki Cole
